source: Bush, R. 2010. 'Large Ruminant Nutrition Theory, Part 2: Silages and Better Feeding Practices', University of Sydney (mekonglivestock.wordpress.com), including a Village Livestock Agent (VLA) fattening-cattle feeding trial conducted in Tbong Khmum, Aug-Dec 2009. text: Farmers are advised to check fattening animals daily for early signs of trouble: a decline in body condition, loss of interest in feed, a dull or rough coat instead of the smooth, shiny coat of a healthy animal, and diarrhoea -- any of these can signal disease, poor nutrition, lack of water, or parasites, and should prompt quick action. Animals should also be checked for ticks and other external parasites and have them removed when found. Additional good practice: clean pens after animals are sold and before new ones move in; keep a little salt in the feed ration or a salt lick available; share fattening experience with other farmers and district staff; check that any newly purchased cattle or buffalo show no obvious disease, and quarantine them for at least 2 weeks before mixing with the existing herd; and handle animals gently and safely, using a sloping ramp when loading onto a truck.
